en: Mahāniddesa,
Aṭṭhakavagga 5.
Paramaṭṭhakasuttaniddesa (The Exposition of the Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta)
Now he will explain the exposition of the *Paramaṭṭhakasutta*:
"Whatever further claim a person makes in this world, while dwelling amidst views as the highest..."
"Low" he says of everything else besides that;
therefore, he has not transcended disputes.
"Supreme" means one who dwells within [wrong] views.
There are some ascetics and brahmins who are followers of speculative views.

Having grasped, taken up, accepted, clung to, and adhered to one or another of the sixty-two types of speculative views, they think: "This is supreme, this is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime."
They dwell, travel, reside, and live according to their respective views.
Just as householders dwell in houses, or those with offenses dwell in their offenses, or those with defilements dwell in their defilements—
even so do some ascetics and brahmins who are followers of speculative views.

Having grasped, taken up, accepted, clung to, and adhered to one or another of those sixty-two views, thinking, "This is supreme, this is the foremost, the best, the most distinguished, the chief, the highest,
the most excellent," they dwell, travel, reside, and live according to their respective views.
Dwelling within views as the ultimate,
whatever further a person claims regarding the world— that is "what" (yad). "That" (iti) refers to that [claim].
“Uttariṁ kurute” means he makes it superior; he makes it foremost, best, distinguished, preeminent, supreme, and excellent.
He makes it superior by thinking, “This Teacher is omniscient”; he makes it foremost, best, distinguished, preeminent, supreme, and excellent.
“This Dhamma is well-expounded... [and so on].
This group has practiced well…;
this view is auspicious…;
this path is well-proclaimed….
"This path leads out"—thus he makes it further; he makes it the foremost, the best, the distinguished, the preeminent, the supreme, the excellent; he produces it, he brings it forth.
"Jantu" means a being, a person... a human being.
"Loka" means the world of the states of loss... up to... the world of the sense bases.
Whatever further a person performs in the world, he says all that is inferior compared to it;
thus, setting aside his own teacher, the proclamation of Dhamma, the assembly, the view, the practice, and the path, he hurls, casts away, and rejects all other doctrines.
"That teacher is not omniscient..."
The Dhamma is not well-expounded;
the community does not practice rightly;
the view is not auspicious.
The practice is not well-proclaimed;
the path does not lead to liberation;
herein there is no purity, nor purification, nor complete purification, nor release, nor liberation, nor total liberation.
"In this there is no cleansing, no purification, no complete purification; no liberation, no release, no total release;

they are inferior, base, low, wretched, fourfold, and limited"—thus he says, thus he speaks, thus he declares, thus he illuminates, thus he expresses it: "inferior" means he says everything other than that.
"Therefore, one who has not transcended disputes":
"therefore" means for that reason, by that cause, by that condition, and by that source.
"Disputes" refers to quarrels regarding views, brawls regarding views, conflicts regarding views, contentions regarding views, and strife regarding views.
"Unsurpassed" means not having transcended, not having overcome, not having gone beyond;
therefore, he has not surpassed disputes.
Thus the Blessed One said:
“Dwelling amidst views as something supreme,
whatever further claim a person makes in this world,
he declares everything else to be inferior.”
"Therefore, one has not transcended disputes.
Whatever benefit one sees for oneself in what is seen,
heard, in moral conduct and vows, or in what is sensed;
Having grasped that very thing there,
he regards everything else as inferior—
whatever benefit he perceives in what is seen, heard, in moral conduct, vows, or what is sensed.
"Whatever is in oneself" means that which is within oneself.
"Self" refers to a speculative view.
One perceives two advantages in one's own view:
The benefit pertaining to the present life and the benefit pertaining to future lives.
What is the benefit for one who holds a particular view pertaining to the present life? Whatever the view of the teacher is, such is the view of his disciples.
The disciples honor, revere, esteem, and worship that teacher who holds such a view; and because of this, they receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
This is the benefit of such a view pertaining to the present life.
What is the benefit of such a view pertaining to future lives?
"This view is sufficient for the state of a nāga, or a supaṇṇa, or a yakkha, or an asura, or a gandhabba, or a great king, or an Indra, or a Brahmā, or a deva;
this view is sufficient for purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, release, and total release;
by means of this view they are purified, purified thoroughly, completely purified, liberated, released, and totally released."
"By means of this view, I shall be purified, cleansed, thoroughly purified; I shall be liberated, fully liberated, completely liberated. Thus, one comes to expect a fruit in the future.
This is the benefit pertaining to the future regarding one's own view.
One sees these two benefits in one's own view, and one also sees two benefits in the purification of one's view.
One sees two benefits in the purification of speech, one sees two benefits in the purification of virtue, one sees two benefits in the purification of conduct,
and one sees two benefits in the purification of intellect—
the benefit pertaining to the present life and the benefit pertaining to the future life.
What is the benefit pertaining to the present life for one who has purified their speech?
Whatever view the teacher holds, his disciples hold that same view...
[and so on] ...this is the benefit pertaining to the present life for one who has purified their speech.
What is the future benefit of purification by verbal expression?
This view is sufficient for the state of a Naga...
[and so on] ...this is the future benefit of purification by verbal expression.
One sees, beholds, looks upon, contemplates, and examines these two benefits even through purity of the mind: namely,
whatever benefit one perceives in oneself regarding what is seen, heard, virtuous conduct, or felt—
that very thing one grasps therein.
"Tadeva" means that very same speculative view.
"Tattha" means by means of one's own view, one's own inclination, one's own preference, and one's own conviction.
"Samuggahāya" means having grasped, taken up, accepted, clung to, and adhered to it as being supreme, foremost, best, distinguished, preeminent, highest, and most excellent.
Having grasped that very thing there, he views everything else as inferior.
He views, sees, beholds, looks upon, contemplates,

and examines another teacher, another proclamation of Dhamma, another assembly, another view, another practice, and another path as inferior, more inferior, low, base, fourth-rate, and limited— this is what is meant by [the term *nihīnato*].
He regards everything else as inferior.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“When he sees for himself the benefit in his own [virtue]...”
Whether in what is seen, heard, in moral conduct and vows, or in what is sensed;
having grasped that very thing there,
he regards every conceit as inferior.
The wise call even that a bond by which,
being dependent on it, one regards another as inferior;
therefore, whatever is seen, heard, or sensed—
“A bhikkhu should not rely upon rules and observances;
the skillful call even that a bond.

As for “the skillful,” they are those who are skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in the foundations of mindfulness.

Skilled in the right efforts, skilled in the bases of psychic power, skilled in the faculties, skilled in the powers, skilled in the factors of enlightenment, skilled in the path, skilled in the fruits, and skilled in Nibbāna, those who are skilled speak thus:
“This is a fetter; this is a snag; this is a bond; this is an impediment.”
"They speak thus, they talk thus, they say thus, they illuminate thus, they express themselves thus"—
the experts call even that a "bond" (gantha).
Dependent upon which, one perceives what is inferior as "other."
"Depending on which" means depending on, relying upon, clinging to, approaching, adhering to, being intent upon, and being devoted to a certain teacher, a proclamation of Dhamma,
a group, a view, a practice, or a path. "He regards another as inferior" means he sees, perceives, beholds, and looks upon another teacher, a proclamation of Dhamma, a group, a view, a practice,
or a path as inferior, low, base, wretched, contemptible, and limited.
"He contemplates, closely contemplates, and examines"—
this refers to that which one relies upon while seeing something else as inferior.
Therefore, a bhikkhu should not rely on what is seen, heard, or sensed, nor on rules and observances.

Therefore, for that reason, on that account, by that condition, and with that as the source, one should not rely upon, nor grasp, nor cling to, nor adhere to what is seen or purification through what is seen;

what is heard or purification through what is heard; what is sensed or purification through what is sensed; or to virtue or purification through virtue; or to observances or purification through observances.
Therefore, a bhikkhu should not rely on what is seen, heard, or sensed, nor on rules and observances.
Thus the Blessed One said:
"The wise call even that a fetter."
Whatever inferior thing one relies upon and sees as superior—
therefore, a bhikkhu should not rely on what is seen, heard, or sensed, nor on rules and observances.
One should not construct views regarding the world,
whether by means of knowledge or even by virtue and observances;
nor should one compare oneself as being equal [to others].
"One should not think oneself inferior, nor superior.
One should not construct views regarding the world, whether by means of knowledge or by means of virtue and observances.

By means of the knowledge of the eight attainments, or the knowledge of the five higher powers, or even wrong knowledge; or by virtue, or observances, or both virtue and observances—one should not construct, generate, produce, bring about, or fully manifest views.
"In the world"— that is, in the world of the states of misery …pe… in the world of the sense bases—
one should not form any view regarding the world, whether by means of knowledge or even by means of virtuous conduct.
One should not lead oneself to think "I am equal."
One should not lead oneself with the thought, "I am equal" on account of birth, or clan, or family lineage,
or physical beauty, or wealth, or Vedic study, or field of occupation, or craft, or branch of science,
or learning, or eloquence, or any other such basis.
One should not compare oneself with an equal;
nor should one think oneself superior or inferior.
One should not apply the thought "I am inferior" to oneself on account of birth, lineage, or any other such basis.
"One should not lead oneself on by thinking, 'I am superior' on account of birth or clan... or on account of any other such basis;
one should not think of oneself as inferior or even as superior.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“One should not construct views regarding the world,
whether by means of knowledge or even by virtue and observances;
one should not lead oneself to think that one is equal [to others].”
“He should not think himself inferior or superior.
Having abandoned the self and grasping nothing,
he does not even rely on knowledge as a support.
He indeed does not side with factions among the learned;
he does not rely on any view whatsoever.
Having abandoned the self, he does not cling.
"Having abandoned self" means having abandoned the view of self.
"Having abandoned self" means having abandoned grasping.

"Having abandoned self" means having abandoned, relinquished, dispelled, brought to an end, and rendered non-existent that which was grasped, adhered to, clung to, obsessed over, and intent upon by way of craving and by way of views.
Having abandoned the self.
"Without clinging" means not clinging, not grasping, not misapprehending, and not adhering by means of the four kinds of clinging;
thus, having abandoned the self, one is without clinging.
"By knowledge he does not provide a support" means that by means of the knowledge of the eight attainments, or the knowledge of the five higher powers,
or wrong knowledge, he does not provide a support for craving or a support for views; he does not produce it, generate it, cause it to arise,
bring it about, or manifest it.
Even by means of his knowledge, he does not take a side. Indeed,
among those who are distinguished, he does not follow a faction— meaning that among those who are divided,
fallen into enmity, fallen into doubt, who hold various views, various inclinations, various tastes, and various convictions, and who rely upon various views as their support.
When others fall into bias through desire, fall into bias through hatred, fall into bias through delusion, or fall into bias through fear, he does not fall into bias through desire,
he does not fall into bias through hatred, he does not fall into bias through delusion, he does not fall into bias through fear;
he does not act under the influence of lust, he does not act under the influence of hatred, and he does not act under the influence of delusion.
He goes by way of human nature, not by way of views, not by way of restlessness, not by way of doubt, and not by way of underlying tendencies;
he is not led, carried away, swept along, or dragged about by factional doctrines—
he indeed does not follow factions among those who are divided.
“He does not rely on any view whatsoever.
For him, the sixty-two types of views have been abandoned, eradicated, stilled, and calmed; they are incapable of arising again, having been consumed by the fire of knowledge.
He does not rely upon, nor does he return to, any type of view whatsoever.
He does not rely on any view whatsoever.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having abandoned the self and not grasping at anything...”
Even by means of knowledge, he does not form a reliance;
indeed, among the learned, he does not follow a faction,
nor does he adhere to any view whatsoever.
For him who has no aspirations here for either of the two ends—
neither for existence nor non-existence, neither in this world nor in the next— there are no attachments whatsoever.
One should thoroughly investigate what has been grasped among phenomena.

For one who has no aspiration here for either of the two extremes—whether for existence or non-existence, in this world or in the next—for such a person, namely the Arahant whose taints are exhausted:
"extreme" refers to contact as one extreme, and the arising of contact as the second extreme.
The past is one extreme, the future is the second extreme;
pleasant feeling is one extreme, painful feeling is the second extreme;
name is one extreme, form is the second extreme.
The six internal sense bases are one extreme; the six external sense bases are the second extreme.
Individuality is one extreme; the origin of individuality is the second extreme.
"Aspiration" is a term for craving.
Whatever lust, infatuation, covetousness, and greed there is—the unwholesome root.

"For becoming and becoming" means for the sake of becoming and becoming: for kamma-becoming and renewed existence; for sensual becoming, kamma-becoming, and renewed existence; for sensual becoming, kamma-becoming, and renewed existence; for fine-material becoming, kamma-becoming, and renewed existence;
for fine-material becoming, kamma-becoming, and renewed existence; for immaterial becoming, kamma-becoming, and renewed existence. For kamma-becoming... [and so on].
For the sake of formless existence, for renewed becoming, for repeated becoming, for repeated destinies, for repeated rebirths, for repeated rebirth-linkings,
and for the repeated production of individuality.
"Here" refers to one's own individuality.
"Hurā" refers to the state of another existence;
"idha" refers to one's own form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness;
"hurā" refers to the form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness of another.
"Here" refers to the six internal sense bases;
"there" refers to the six external sense bases;
"here" refers to the world of human beings.
"Hurā" refers to the world of the devas;
"idha" refers to the realm of sense-desire (kāmadhātu),
while "hurā" refers to the realm of form (rūpadhātu) and the formless realm (arūpadhātu).
"Here" refers to the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the fine-material realm (*rūpadhātu*).
"Thereafter" refers to the immaterial realm (*arūpadhātu*).
For one who has no aspiration here for either of these two ends—neither for existence nor non-existence, neither here nor thereafter.
For whom there is no longing for both ends—for existence and non-existence, here or hereafter;

for whom such craving does not exist, does not persist, is not found, and is not apprehended; which has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided, incapable of arising again, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—for whom there is no longing here for either of these two ends, whether for existence or non-existence, here or hereafter.
"He has no dwellings whatsoever.
"Dwellings" refers to two kinds of dwellings:
the dwelling of craving and the dwelling of views... [etc.]...
This is the settling in craving... [and so on] ...this is the settling in views.
"Of him" means of the arahant whose taints are destroyed.
“Of him there are no attachments whatsoever”: for him there are no attachments whatsoever; they do not exist, they are not found, they are not present, they are not obtained.
They have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, calmed, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt away by the fire of knowledge—thus, “of him there are no attachments whatsoever.”
"Having thoroughly determined among the phenomena" means:
"among the phenomena" refers to the sixty-two types of speculative views.
"Having thoroughly determined" means having decided, having analyzed, having investigated, having scrutinized, having weighed, having judged, having clarified, and having made manifest.

“Comprehended” means: grasped by way of a downward sweep, grasped by way of a cavity, grasped by way of a peak, grasped by way of a portion, grasped by way of accumulation, or grasped by way of total collection;

that which has been taken up, clung to, adhered to, obsessed over, and intent upon as “this is true, real, such, factual, as it is, and not otherwise”—that [view] does not exist, is not present, is not found, is not obtained; it is abandoned and utterly cut off.
"Stilled, calmed, incapable of arising again, and burnt away by the fire of knowledge"—
thus one has discerned and grasped the truth among all phenomena.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“For one who has no aspirations here for either of the two ends—
neither for existence nor non-existence in this world or the next—
for such a person there are no attachments whatsoever.”
"Having thoroughly investigated phenomena, one has grasped what is truly so.
In this world, regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed,
there is not even the slightest notion that has been preconceived.
Not adopting the views of that brahmin,
who in this world could form a conceptualization? For him,
here in what is seen, heard, or sensed, there is not even the slightest perception that has been constructed.
"Of him" means of the arahant whose taints are destroyed.
Whether regarding what is seen, for the sake of purity in what is seen; or regarding what is heard, for the sake of purity in what is heard;

or regarding what is sensed, for the sake of purity in what is sensed—therein, his state of being preceded by perception, his state of conceptualizing through perception, and that which is raised up and fully established by perception through the grasping of perception [prevails].
"Fabricated, fashioned, conditioned, constructed, and established; views do not exist, they are not present, they are not found, they are not obtained;

they are abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge"—thus, here in this world, regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed, there is not even the slightest notion that has been fabricated.

"Without heeding that brahmin’s view. He is called a "brahmin" because he has banished seven things—a brahmin is one for whom the personality-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) has been banished... [and so on] ...up to... the conceit "I am. Without heeding such a brahmin’s view, one should not adopt it. One should not say: "This is the truth, all else is false. Why? Because that view is unwholesome, blameworthy, and leads to suffering; it is not conducive to the goal, nor to what is wholesome, nor to Nirvana. Because that view is unwholesome, blameworthy, and leads to suffering; it is not conducive to the goal, nor to what is wholesome, nor to Nirvana. Therefore, without heeding that
"One who is unshaken is called such, he is a Brahmā.
Not taking up the views of that brahmin"—
meaning not taking up, not grasping, not clinging to, and not adhering to the views of that brahmin.
Not adopting the views of that brahmin, who in this world could form a conceptual construction?
There are two kinds of constructions: [the construction of eternity and the construction of annihilation].
The conceptualization of craving and the conceptualization of views...
[as before] ...this is the conceptualization of craving... [as before] ...this is the conceptualization of views.
For him, the construction of craving has been abandoned and the construction of views has been relinquished.
Because the construction of craving has been abandoned and the construction of views has been relinquished, by what lust would he construct?
By what hatred would he construct? By what delusion would he construct? By what conceit would he construct? By what view would he construct?
By what restlessness would it be constructed? By what doubt would it be constructed?

By which underlying tendencies would it be constructed—that is, as "lustful," or "hateful," or "deluded," or "bound," or "misapprehended," or "distracted," or "fallen into the undesirable," or "become firm"?
Those volitional formations have been abandoned.

With the abandoning of volitional formations, by what means could one conceive of destinies—whether as a denizen of hell, or an animal, or a ghost, or a human, or a deva; or as having form, or being formless; or as percipient, or non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient?
There is no cause, no condition, no reason by which one could conceive, could differentiate, or could fall into such conceptualization.
"In the world": in the world of the states of misery …pe… in the world of the sense-bases—who here in the world could conceptualize?
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“In this world, regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed,
there is not even the slightest perception constructed [by him].
Not grasping at views, that one is a brahmin.”
"What could one construct here in this world?
They do not construct, they do not hold things before them,
and even phenomena are not grasped by them.
A brahmin is not to be led by mere virtuous conduct;
one who has gone to the further shore does not return, for such a person is "one who is thus.
They do not construct conceptual fabrications, nor do they hold things as foremost.
"Kappa" refers to two types of kappa:
the kappa of craving (taṇhākappa) and the kappa of views (diṭṭhikappa).
What is the kappa of craving?
To whatever extent it has been delimited, defined by boundaries, established as a range, circumscribed, grasped, and claimed as "mine"—namely:
"This is mine; this belongs to me; this much is mine; to this extent is mine"—such as forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles;
rugs and coverlets; female and male slaves; goats, sheep, chickens, pigs, elephants, cattle, horses, and mares.
Fields, lands, gold, silver, villages, towns, royal capitals, kingdoms, districts,
treasuries, and storehouses— even the entire great earth— one regards as "mine" through the influence of craving; as far as the eighty-four thousand modes of the movement of craving extend—
this is the "world of craving."
What is the conceptualization of views?
It is the embodiment-view based on twenty bases, the wrong view based on ten bases, and the extreme-view based on ten bases;
whatever view there is of such a kind—this is called a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a contortion of views, a vacillation of views, and a fetter of views.
The fetter of views, grasping, seizing upon, insistence, misapprehension, the wrong path, the false road, falsity,

the domain of sectarian teachers, the grasping of inversion, the grasping of what is perverted, the grasping of distortion, wrong grasping, the grasping of what is not as it really is as being as it really is—
in short, the sixty-two types of speculative views.
This is the conceptualization of views.
For them, the conceptualization of craving has been abandoned and the conceptualization of views has been relinquished.

Because the conceptualization of craving has been abandoned and the conceptualization of views has been relinquished, they do not construct, generate, produce, bring forth, or cause to arise either the conceptualization of craving or the conceptualization of views.
They do not fashion [conceptions].
They do not hold in high esteem.
There are two kinds of holding in high esteem:
There is that which has craving as its primary focus and that which has views as its primary focus...
[as above] ...this is that which has craving as its primary focus... [as above] ...this is that which has views as its primary focus.
For them, the prioritizing of craving has been abandoned, and the prioritizing of views has been relinquished.

Because the prioritizing of craving has been abandoned and the prioritizing of views has been relinquished, they do not proceed making either craving or views their forerunner; they do not have craving as their banner, craving as their standard, nor craving as their sovereign.
They do not have views as their banner, nor views as their standard, nor views as their sovereign. They do not wander surrounded by craving or views;
thus they do not construct [fictions] and do not hold them foremost.
"Even teachings are not accepted by them.
"Teachings" refers to the sixty-two types of speculative views.
"By them" means by those Arahants whose taints are destroyed.
He does not adhere to the view: “The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false. He does not adhere to the view:
“The world is non-eternal… the world is finite… [the world is infinite]…”
The world is infinite … that the soul is the same as the body … that the soul is one thing and the body another …
Does the Tathāgata exist after death?
Does the Tathāgata not exist after death?
Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death?
“‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is vain’—he does not hold such a view;
thus even their doctrines are not held.
A brahmin is not to be led by mere virtue.”
This is not a denial.
One is a brahmin because of having banished seven things—a brahmin because the view of a personal body has been banished... [and so on] ...up to... [the conceit "I am"] has been banished.
One who is thus unshaken is called a brahmin.
A brahmin is not led by virtue, nor by vows, nor by virtue-and-vows.
This means that a brahmin is not led, not guided, not carried away, and not swept along by virtue, or by vows, or by virtue-and-vows.
"A brahmin is not to be led by mere observance of moral precepts.
One who has gone to the further shore, such a one as he, does not return.
By "the further shore" is meant the deathless Nibbāna.

That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna—that is one who has gone to the further shore, reached the further shore, gone to the end, reached the end, gone to the limit, reached the limit. (In detail: regarding the cycle of birth and death, for him there is no further becoming—thus he is "one who has gone to the further shore."
"He does not return" means: those defilements abandoned by the path of stream-entry, he does not repeat them, does not return to them, does not go back to them.
Those defilements abandoned by the path of once-returning, he does not repeat them, does not return to them, does not go back to them.
Those defilements abandoned by the path of non-returning, he does not repeat them, does not return to them, does not go back to them.
Those defilements which have been abandoned by the path of arahantship—he does not bring them back, he does not return to them, he does not go back to them;
thus, having gone to the further shore, he does not return.
"Such" (tādī) means that the arahant is "such" in five ways:
One who is such toward the desirable and the undesirable is "such" (tādī); one who has abandoned [them] is "such"; one who has crossed over [them] is "such";

one who is liberated [from them] is "such"; because of that designation, he is "such. How is the Arahant "such" toward the desirable and the undesirable? The Arahant is "such" in gain and "such" in loss; "such" in fame and "such" in disrepute; "such" in praise and "such" in blame; "such" in pleasure and "such" in pain.
If they were to smear one arm with perfume and carve the other arm with an adze—
there is no lust for the one, and no aversion for the other; having abandoned both attraction and repulsion, having shaken off and overcome them, and having transcended compliance and resistance—
the Arahant is thus the same toward the pleasant and the unpleasant.
How is it that the Arahant is one who has abandoned [defilements] and is such-like (tādī)?
In the Arahant, lust is abandoned, vomited out, released, relinquished, and discarded.
Hatred… [and so forth].
delusion … anger … malice …
Deceit … hypocrisy … envy …
Avarice … deceit … craftiness …
Arrogance … hostility … conceit …
excessive pride … intoxication … negligence …
All defilements … all misconducts … all distresses …
All fevers...
all torments...
all unwholesome volitional formations have been vomited up, released, abandoned, and relinquished.
Thus the Arahant is "one who has crossed over," a "Tādi.
How is the Arahant "one who has crossed over," a "Tādi"?

The Arahant has crossed over the flood of sensual desire, crossed over the flood of existence, crossed over the flood of views, and crossed over the flood of ignorance; he has crossed over the entire path of saṃsāra—he has crossed it, gone beyond it, transcended it, surpassed it, and passed completely beyond it.
Thus, having completed his residence [in the training], having practiced the conduct, and having ended the saṃsāra of birth and death, there is no further becoming for him.
In this way, the Arahant is "one who has crossed over," thus he is "such" (tādī). How is the Arahant "one who is liberated," thus he is "such"?
The mind of the Arahant is liberated, released, and well-released from lust;
the mind is liberated, released, and well-released from hatred;
the mind is liberated, released, and well-released from delusion.
Anger … resentment … contempt …
... from malice ...
from envy ...
from stinginess ...
...deceit,
...guile,
...obstinacy...
... with instigation ...
with conceit ...
with overweening pride ...
...from intoxication ... from negligence ...
from all defilements ...
... from all forms of misconduct ...
from all anxieties ...
from all fevers ...
The mind is released, liberated, and well-liberated from all fevers and from all unwholesome volitional formations.
Thus the Arahant is one who has attained liberation and is such-like.
How is the Arahant “such” (tādī) by virtue of being designated by that [very quality]?
When virtue is present, the Arahant is “virtuous”; thus he is such by virtue of being designated by that.
When faith is present, he is “faithful”; thus he is such by virtue of being designated by that.
When there is energy, one is "possessed of energy"—such is the description of that person.
When there is mindfulness, one is "possessed of mindfulness"—such is the description of that person.
When there is concentration, one is "concentrated"—such is the description of that person.
When wisdom exists, one is "possessed of wisdom" because of that designation;
when true knowledge exists, one is "possessed of the three knowledges" because of that designation;
when direct knowledge exists, one is "possessed of the six direct knowledges" because of that designation.
Thus the Arahant, described by that term, is "the Stable One" (tādī)—
one who has gone to the further shore and does not return.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“They do not construct [concepts], nor do they hold them foremost;
even phenomena are not concealed from them.
A brahmin is not to be led by mere virtue and observances.”
“One who has gone beyond does not return; such a one is the Tathāgata.
The fifth exposition: the Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta.
